title: Sex and gender differences in substance use disorders

claims.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether women in general go from first use of alcohol or other drugs to dependence, or to treatment, faster than men (the idea called 'telescoping'): the faster course was described in people in treatment and self-help groups, from ages they recalled years later, and the one general-population test read here, for alcohol, did not find the full pattern. In two pooled US national household surveys (NLAES, 1991–1992, response 90%, and NESARC, 2001–2002, response 81%; 53,238 US-born adults aged 18 to 57; every age recalled at a single interview), women had their first drink later than men (on average at 19.0 against 17.8 years; the gap narrowed from 3.0 years in people born 1934–1943 to 0.4 years in those born 1974–1983). Among all 38,309 people who had ever drunk, men had a higher hazard of alcohol dependence than women in every birth cohort (hazard ratios 1.36 to 1.79, adjusted for survey, race and ethnicity, income, education, urbanicity and age at first drink); since the times below were similar, this mostly reflects men's higher chance of ever becoming dependent, not faster progression. Among the people who did become dependent, the group whose timing treatment-sample studies measure, the average time from first drink to dependence was about the same in women and men (5.6 against 5.8 years; unadjusted) and shorter in women born 1964–1973 (3.7 against 4.2 years). Among people with dependence, men also had a higher hazard of first alcohol treatment, significantly in two of five birth cohorts (1.55 and 1.42) (Keyes et al., 2010). The authors conclude that telescoping is not evident in the general population, although their Discussion's statement that women were faster on neither measure goes further than their own table. As described in a historical critique, the idea goes back to a 1952 WHO committee report and to stage models built from the recalled drinking histories of 98 men in Alcoholics Anonymous, with 15 women's answers set aside; the 1989 study that named telescoping timed 33 women and 105 men from treatment programmes and self-help groups, in whom the interval from first alcohol-related problem to first treatment was 4.3 years shorter in women; 75 of 103 articles citing that study used it as background without testing it; and the critique's authors recommend dropping the term (Marks & Clark, 2018). Narrative reviews by one research group list faster progression in women for alcohol, cannabis, cocaine and prescription opioids, but not heroin, mostly in treatment samples (McHugh et al., 2018, which explains the difference from population surveys by who reaches treatment; Greenfield et al., 2007, which calls it one of the most reproducible findings); a national sample of 1,217 women and 3,297 men is described, without its timing measure or adjustment, as finding the time from first cannabis use to cannabis use disorder 2.5 years shorter in women (Khan et al., 2013, as described by Marks & Clark, 2018). Randall et al. (1999), the Project MATCH treatment-sample study, which the papers read describe in opposite ways, is not yet read. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claims.magnitude: Not estimable as a general difference in speed. General-population surveys, alcohol (Keyes et al., 2010): age at first drink, women 19.0 vs men 17.8 years (gap 3.0 years in people born 1934–1943, 0.4 in those born 1974–1983; editors' subtraction); hazard of dependence among all lifetime drinkers, men vs women, 1.56 (95% CI 1.35–1.79), 1.36 (1.23–1.50), 1.46 (1.33–1.62), 1.79 (1.58–2.02) and 1.71 (1.34–2.20) for people born 1974–1983, 1964–1973, 1954–1963, 1944–1953 and 1934–1943 (a mixture of the chance of dependence and its speed); mean time from first drink to dependence among people who became dependent (unadjusted), women 5.6 vs men 5.8 years (ratio 1.04, not significant), born 1964–1973 3.7 vs 4.2 years (p = 0.02), born 1954–1963 5.5 vs 6.4 years (not marked significant; t about 2.4 from the printed means and standard errors, an editors' approximation on the study card); hazard of first treatment among people with dependence, men vs women, 1.16 (0.77–1.76), 1.55 (1.22–1.96), 1.42 (1.16–1.73), 1.20 (0.91–1.58) and 1.38 (0.84–2.26) in the same cohort order; mean time from dependence to first treatment among people treated, born 1934–1943, women 19.4 vs men 23.5 years (the overall means, 6.1 vs 7.0, cannot be reconciled with the cohort rows and are not used). Treatment and self-help samples, second-hand (Marks & Clark, 2018): founding study, 33 women and 105 men, first problem to first treatment 4.3 years shorter in women, first drink about 2 and first intoxication about 3 years later in women, same age at treatment entry; Iowa treatment centres (3,132 men, 395 women), treatment about 2 years after a first attempt to quit in women, about 3 in men; national cannabis sample (1,217 women, 3,297 men), first use to cannabis use disorder 2.5 years shorter in women; 75 of 103 citing articles used the founding study as background.

claims.statement: In US national household surveys, women with alcohol dependence compared with men with alcohol dependence were less likely, or slower, to reach alcohol treatment in the years after their problems began, while for drug use disorders, and for treatment in the past year, no gender difference was described; treatment was uncommon for both. In two pooled general-population surveys (NLAES, 1991–1992, and NESARC, 2001–2002; 8,564 US-born adults aged 18 to 57 with alcohol dependence; ages at onset and at first treatment recalled at a single interview), the hazard of first alcohol treatment was higher in men than in women in all five birth cohorts, significantly in people born 1954–1963 (hazard ratio 1.42, 95% CI 1.16 to 1.73) and 1964–1973 (1.55, 1.22 to 1.96), with intervals including no difference in the other three (adjusted for survey, race and ethnicity, income, education, urbanicity and age at first drink); about a quarter (24.6%) of people with dependence had ever had any alcohol treatment; among people who were treated, women born 1934–1943 reached treatment sooner after dependence began (19.4 against 23.5 years) (Keyes et al., 2010). As described by a narrative review, an earlier analysis of the 1991–1992 survey (Dawson, 1996; 7,359 people with alcohol abuse or dependence; onset and treatment reported after the fact; adjustment not described) found that 23% of men and 15.1% of women had ever been treated (counting a doctor, counsellor, Alcoholics Anonymous, another professional or a treatment facility), with no gender difference in the first 8 years after onset, men 13% to 20% more likely to start treatment between 8 and 25 years after onset, and no difference among the most severely dependent; past-year alcohol treatment among people with alcohol dependence was 12.5% in women and 12.1% in men in a 1999 household survey, and gender was not associated with past-year use of substance use services in the 2002 national survey (Greenfield et al., 2007, second-hand). Women were a smaller share of people in US alcohol treatment than of people with alcohol use disorders (men to women 3.3 to 1 in treatment facilities against 2.7 to 1 in the population in 1991), and women with drinking problems more often sought help in mental-health and other non-specialist services; barriers documented for women include childcare, pregnancy and fear of losing custody or of prosecution, stigma and co-occurring mental-health problems (Greenfield et al., 2007). A later review reports, from the 2015 national survey, that 10.4% of women and 11.1% of men who needed treatment for an alcohol or drug use disorder received it, that under-treatment was most marked among women with alcohol use disorder, and that gender was not associated with treatment use for illicit drug use disorders (McHugh et al., 2018, second-hand). The two analyses of the 1991–1992 survey share data and are not independent; all timing and treatment were self-reported, years later; 'treatment' was defined differently across studies; and the figures are from the USA. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team (two analyses that share a survey).
claims.magnitude: Keyes et al. (2010), hazard of first alcohol treatment among people with dependence, men vs women (Cox, adjusted): born 1974–1983 1.16 (95% CI 0.77–1.76), 1964–1973 1.55 (1.22–1.96), 1954–1963 1.42 (1.16–1.73), 1944–1953 1.20 (0.91–1.58), 1934–1943 1.38 (0.84–2.26); 24.6% of people with dependence ever treated (possibly weighted; 3,056 of 8,564 unweighted, about 36%, editors' arithmetic on the study card); among people treated, born 1934–1943, mean time from dependence to first treatment women 19.4 vs men 23.5 years. Second-hand: NLAES 1992 (Dawson, 1996), ever treated men 23% vs women 15.1%, cumulative probability by 30 years after onset .424 vs .356, no difference up to 8 years, men 13–20% more likely between 8 and 25 years, men-to-women ratio 1.75:1 with one symptom and 1.24:1 with 15 symptoms; past-year alcohol treatment among people with alcohol dependence (1999 household survey, 32,628 people) women 12.5% vs men 12.1%; men to women in US alcohol treatment 3.3:1 against 2.7:1 for alcohol use disorders in the population (1991), and 2.3:1 in facilities (2002) against 1.9:1 for past-year alcohol dependence and 1.5:1 for illicit drug dependence (2003) (Greenfield et al., 2007); 2015 national survey, treatment received among people needing it, women 10.4% vs men 11.1% (McHugh et al., 2018).

claims.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether women and men who enter treatment for alcohol or other drug use disorders differ in how long they stay or how well they do: as summarized by two narrative reviews from one research group, most large studies found no gender difference in retention, completion or outcome, and where a difference appeared it more often favoured women; the reviews' figures are second-hand. A review of 280 articles published from 1975 to 2005 (11.8% of them randomized trials; the studies were not appraised) describes large multi-programme data sets with very few gender differences in retention (among 10,010 patients in 96 programmes, men were 20% less likely than women to stay 90 days in outpatient drug-free care; in a national study of 4,689 adults, gender was not associated with completion after adjustment), small clinical studies that disagreed in both directions, and outcome studies that mostly found no difference (in one study of older adults in outpatient alcohol treatment, 79.3% of women and 54% of men were abstinent at 6 months, a difference that disappeared after adjustment for length of stay) (Greenfield et al., 2007). The group's 2018 update describes no gender difference in outcome in large randomized trials (COMBINE, 1,226 people with alcohol dependence, 31% women; a prescription-opioid trial, 653 people, 40% women), none in retention across 24 NIDA Clinical Trials Network trials (more than 11,000 people), and none in completion across more than 1.7 million US treatment episodes, except that women less often completed detoxification; smoking cessation is the exception, with worse outcomes in women, and for disulfiram the effect in women is unknown because women were, for example, 1.2% of trial participants (McHugh et al., 2018). Randomized comparisons of women-only with mixed-gender programmes were few and mixed, and changing a programme to women-only did not by itself change outcomes; in the one randomized comparison of outcomes described, a hospital mixed-gender programme had higher abstinence than a women-only day programme (Greenfield et al., 2007), and the group's own larger trial found its women-focused group as effective as mixed-gender counselling, not more (McHugh et al., 2018). These comparisons are between women and men who had already entered treatment; within trials, women and men were compared as subgroups, not assigned at random; outcomes were defined in many different ways; a non-significant difference is not evidence that outcomes are the same; and several of the analyses are the reviewers' own. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Second-hand, none pooled, mostly without intervals. Greenfield et al. (2007): 280 articles 1975–2005, 11.8% randomized trials; 10,010 patients in 96 programmes, men 20% less likely to stay 90 days in outpatient drug-free care; 26,047 patients in 87 Los Angeles programmes, women more often completed where differences appeared; 4,689 adults (1,239 women), gender not associated with completion after adjustment; older adults, abstinence in the past 30 days at 6 months 79.3% of women vs 54% of men, not significant after adjustment for length of stay. McHugh et al. (2018): COMBINE (n = 1,226, 31% women) and a prescription-opioid trial (n = 653, 40% women), no gender difference in outcome; 24 Clinical Trials Network trials (n > 11,000), no difference in retention; more than 1.7 million treatment episodes, no difference in completion except detoxification (women less often); smoking cessation worse in women; women 1.2% of participants in the disulfiram trials cited as an example.
